strengths: Sound theoretical grounding using semiparametric efficiency and efficient influence functions (EIF) to achieve provable variance reduction in LLM evaluation.
Clever framing of pairwise comparison signals from LLM judges as control variates to extract additional signal from small-sample benchmarks.
Consistent empirical improvements across synthetic setups and standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, GSM8K).
weaknesses: Incurs substantial additional computational and inference overhead due to generating auxiliary reasoning paths and gathering pairwise preferences.
The semantic regressor heuristic using prompted LLMs for small sample sizes lacks rigorous theoretical analysis regarding bias propagation.
Real-world evaluations focus on subsampled subsets rather than exploring broader task distributions beyond mathematical and scientific QA.

strengths: Applies semiparametric efficiency theory and efficient influence functions (EIF) in a novel way to address sample-size limitations and variance in LLM evaluation.
Provides formal theoretical guarantees, including asymptotic normality and guaranteed variance reduction when auxiliary signals are informative.
Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements over naive sample means across both synthetic simulations and real-world benchmarks (GPQA, AIME 2025, GSM8K).
weaknesses: Introducing multiple auxiliary generations and pairwise evaluations significantly increases inference cost and token overhead relative to standard evaluation.
Using a large LLM as a 'semantic regressor' in small-sample regimes lacks formal non-parametric convergence guarantees and may introduce unmodeled bias.
Empirical validation benchmarks use the empirical full-set mean as ground truth rather than true population expectations, limiting the assessment of finite-sample bias.

strengths: Principled formalization of LLM accuracy evaluation using semiparametric inference and the efficient influence function (EIF).
Solid theoretical backing establishing asymptotic normality and variance reduction over naive sample averaging.
Creative use of model verification abilities and pairwise judgments over auxiliary responses as control variates to address benchmark sample constraints.
weaknesses: High computational overhead incurred by repeatedly sampling auxiliary reasoning chains and eliciting pairwise judgments.
Theoretical gap in small-sample regimes where cross-fitting is substituted by heuristic prompting of an off-the-shelf LLM semantic regressor.
Empirical variance reduction is modest on several benchmarks, occasionally degrading performance relative to the sample ground truth.

strengths: Novel and elegant conceptual framing: Framing LLM evaluation with auxiliary comparative signals as a semiparametric inference problem with a known conditional distribution p(Z|X) (generated via on-demand sampling) is mathematically principled and creative.

Rigorous theoretical development: The derivation of the Efficient Influence Function (EIF), asymptotic normality, and conditions for strict variance reduction under semiparametric theory are clearly presented and sound.

Strong motivation: Addressing the high variance and brittleness of small-benchmark evaluation (such as AIME with N=30) by exploiting the generation-verification gap is practically relevant and timely.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts controlled simulations as well as extensive experiments across multiple real-world benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, GSM8K) and 10 diverse LLMs, backed by multiple sensitivity and robustness checks (varying auxiliary models, seeds, subset sizes, and prompts).
weaknesses: Theoretical gap regarding the 'Semantic Regressor': In Section 3.2 (Remark 3.5) and Algorithm 2, the authors replace the cross-fitted estimator with a fixed zero-shot LLM (Gemini-3-Flash). Under this setup, Assumption 4.2 (L2 consistency of tau_hat to tau) cannot hold as N -> infinity because the regressor is fixed and not updated. While the estimator remains strictly unbiased for any fixed tau_hat due to the control variate property E[m_hat - tau_hat] = 0, it no longer achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound, and variance reduction is no longer guaranteed if tau_hat is poorly correlated with the outcome.

Experimental evaluation protocol vs. practical evaluation: In Section 5.2, the method is evaluated by subsampling N=15 out of 30 problems on AIME (or N=50 on GPQA) and treating the full-dataset naive mean as ground truth. In realistic deployment, practitioners have all N=30 problems and face run-to-run sampling variance of LLM generations. Demonstrating variance reduction over repeated full-benchmark runs (evaluating true generation stochasticity across seeds) would provide more direct evidential support than subset-to-full subsampling.

Computational overhead and token budget: The method queries M+1 auxiliary reasoning pairs and requires M+1 pairwise comparisons by the target model, along with M+1 calls to the semantic regressor. While Table 6 compares against an equal-sample repeated-Y baseline (12 target generations), pairwise verification inputs include problem text plus two full candidate solutions (often thousands of tokens), which can incur significantly greater prompt token consumption than generating answers directly. A more thorough token-level FLOP/cost accounting is warranted.

strengths: Principled and innovative formulation: Casting LLM benchmark evaluation into a semiparametric inference framework and treating pairwise comparison signals as control variates is a highly original and well-motivated conceptual contribution.

Rigor of theoretical analysis: The derivation of the Efficient Influence Function (EIF) under the AI evaluation setting—where the conditional distribution of auxiliary signals given the input prompt is known and sampleable—is clean, mathematically rigorous, and fully supported by comprehensive proofs in the appendix.

Timely practical relevance: Evaluating reasoning LLMs on small, expert-curated benchmarks (e.g., AIME with N=30) suffers from severe stochasticity and high variance; this work offers a statistically grounded variance-reduction methodology that does not require expanding test set size.

Extensive empirical and robustness validation: The evaluation covers simulations, multiple benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, GSM8K), 10 state-of-the-art models, various auxiliary model pairings, alternative judging rubrics, seed perturbations, and an equal-budget comparison with repeated decoding.
weaknesses: Theoretical gap in the small-sample zero-shot regressor implementation: Theorem 4.5 requires Assumption 4.2 (L2 consistency of the nuisance estimator $\hat{\tau}$ to $\tau$), whereas in practice (Algorithm 2 and Section 5.2) an off-the-shelf LLM (Gemini-3-Flash) is used zero-shot as $\hat{\tau}$. While the estimator remains unbiased because $\hat{m}(X)$ is formed by integrating the same $\hat{\tau}$, the consistency condition for semiparametric efficiency bound attainment is unlikely to hold strictly for a fixed zero-shot LLM, which warrants clearer distinction in the text.

Computational overhead and API costs: Constructing auxiliary pairs, querying the target model for pairwise preferences $M$ times, and querying the semantic regressor $M$ times per instance incurs non-negligible inference overhead. Although Table 6 provides an equal-budget comparison on GPQA, a more holistic cost-benefit analysis (e.g., token consumption, latency, and monetary cost) across tasks would strengthen the practical recommendations.

Finite-sample degradation on very weak models: As seen in Table 2 for AIME 2025 (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct), the one-step estimator occasionally yields negative improvements over the naive estimator. A deeper characterization of the regime where the target model's comparative signal degrades to pure noise would be beneficial.

strengths: Principled and creative formulation: The paper introduces a novel perspective by framing LLM benchmark evaluation through the lens of semiparametric inference, utilizing the 'generation-verification gap' (pairwise comparisons) as auxiliary control variates.

Rigorous theoretical derivations: Under the specified semiparametric model space where the auxiliary conditional distribution p(Z|X) is known, the orthogonal projection onto the tangent space, the derivation of the Efficient Influence Function (EIF, Proposition 3.3), and the proof of asymptotic normality (Theorem 4.5) and strict variance reduction (Corollary 4.7) are theoretically sound.

Comprehensive experimental scope: The authors evaluate the approach across a wide range of models (both open and proprietary) and benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, GSM8K), accompanied by extensive sensitivity and robustness checks varying auxiliary model pairings, random seeds, subset sizes, and prompt rubrics.
weaknesses: Theoretical-to-practical disconnect in nuisance estimation: The central theoretical results (Theorem 4.5 and the attainment of the semiparametric efficiency bound) fundamentally rely on Assumption 4.2, which requires the nuisance estimator tau_hat to be L2-consistent for tau. In practice (Remark 3.5 and Algorithm 2), the authors discard regression fitting and instead substitute a zero-shot prompt to Gemini-3-Flash as a fixed 'semantic regressor'. A frozen zero-shot LLM prompt does not converge to the true conditional expectation E[phi(Y, G) | X, Z] as N grows, meaning the estimator does not achieve the theoretical semiparametric efficiency bound. While the one-step estimator remains unbiased (since E[m_hat(X) - tau_hat(X, Z) | X] = 0 identically for any fixed tau_hat), fixing the control variate coefficient to 1 without estimating the optimal scaling factor can inflate variance if tau_hat is poorly calibrated or weakly correlated.

Unrealistic evaluation setup for small-sample benchmarks: A central motivating premise is that benchmarks like AIME 2025 are size-constrained (N = 30). However, the experimental design evaluates a subsample of N = 15 problems to estimate the full N = 30 accuracy. In real-world evaluation, practitioners already possess all 30 problems and evaluate them directly. Moreover, the claim in Section C.6 that running the one-step estimator on the full N = 30 dataset 'reveals a performance advantage' for GPT-5.2 over Gemini-3-Flash (where both achieved identical 29/30 ground truth) is unsubstantiated speculation, as there is no ground-truth superpopulation metric against which to validate that ranking shift.

Unfair compute and resource accounting: In Section 5.3 (Table 6), the authors present an 'equal-budget' comparison against a 12-sample repeated decoding baseline (12 target generations). However, computing the one-step estimator requires 1 target generation, 11 target pairwise judgments, 22 auxiliary model generations (e.g., GPT-5 mini / DeepSeek-V3.2), and 11 evaluator model calls (Gemini-3-Flash). Counting only target queries ignores the massive additional computational and financial overhead of the 33 auxiliary LLM calls per problem, rendering the 'equal-budget' claim misleading.

Mixed performance against repeated decoding: Even within the target-only budget comparison in Table 6, for DeepSeek-V3.2(Thinking), the 12-Y baseline achieves an absolute error of 1.68%, whereas the one-step estimator exhibits substantially larger errors (3.95% under Config 1 and 5.95% under Config 2), contradicting the assertion that the one-step estimator is consistently superior under equal target query budgets.

Marginal practical gains on standard benchmarks: On datasets like GSM8K (Table 3), the absolute difference between the naive sample mean and the one-step estimator is often negligible (e.g., +0.10% to +0.35%), with models already clustering at >93–98% accuracy. The high complexity and API overhead of orchestrating multi-model auxiliary generations are difficult to justify for such marginal corrections.
